concept.name: gRPC & Streaming RPC

relationships.description: Connects gRPC & Streaming RPC to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: gRPC multiplexes strongly typed Protobuf messages over persistent HTTP/2 streams, supporting unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, and full-duplex bidirectional RPCs.
spark.keyTakeaway: gRPC cuts serialization and connection overhead for internal microservices and real-time streams, but HTTP/2's single-TCP-connection multiplexing breaks naive L4 load balancing.

concept.whyItMatters: REST/JSON over HTTP/1.1 wastes CPU parsing text keys and stalls behind head-of-line connection limits when microservices chat thousands of times per second. gRPC uses binary Protocol Buffers (`proto3`) over HTTP/2, packing dozens of concurrent RPCs and long-lived bidirectional streams onto one TLS connection with built-in deadlines (`grpc-timeout`), cancellation propagation, and flow control.
whenToUse: Internal service-to-service communication in polyglot stacks (Go, Java, Python, Rust) where strict `.proto` contracts and 3–10x smaller payloads matter.
Real-time streaming pipelines—live telemetry ingestion, LLM token streaming, or financial order-book ticks—using server or bidirectional streaming.
Low-latency mobile-to-edge or edge-to-core APIs that benefit from HPACK header compression and deadline propagation across call trees.
whenNotToUse: Direct browser-to-backend calls without a proxy; browsers do not expose raw HTTP/2 trailers (`grpc-status`), requiring gRPC-Web translation via Envoy.
Public third-party APIs where human-readable `curl` debugging, OpenAPI tooling, and HTTP caching semantics matter more than binary efficiency.
Simple CRUD services with low QPS (< 100 RPS) where JSON/REST keeps debugging and schema evolution effortless.
keyPoints: Every gRPC message is wrapped in a 5-byte Length-Prefixed Message frame inside HTTP/2 `DATA` frames: 1 byte compression flag + 4-byte big-endian uint32 length + Protobuf bytes.

HTTP/2 `HEADERS` carry `:path` (`/package.Service/Method`) and `grpc-timeout` (e.g., `500m`), while a trailing `HEADERS` frame (`END_STREAM`) delivers `grpc-status` (e.g., `0` OK, `4` DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, `14` UNAVAILABLE).
HTTP/2 flow control (`WINDOW_UPDATE` frames, 64 KiB default window) applies backpressure per stream and per connection so a slow consumer cannot OOM a fast producer.
Because HTTP/2 pins multiple RPCs to one long-lived TCP connection, L4 TCP load balancers route all traffic to a single pod; you must use L7-aware balancing (Envoy, Linkerd, or client-side xDS).
Protobuf wire format tags fields by integer field number (varints, 64-bit, length-delimited) rather than field names—making field renames free while making tag reuse a silent data-corruption bug.

examples.title: Bidirectional streaming for real-time voice transcription
examples.scenario: A mobile app streams 20 ms Opus audio chunks to an ASR service while receiving partial word hypotheses back before the user finishes speaking.
examples.outcome: A single `rpc StreamTranscribe(stream AudioChunk) returns (stream TranscriptEvent)` keeps one HTTP/2 stream open. The client sends 50 frames/sec (~400 bytes each) while the server pushes interim and final transcripts on the same stream, cutting end-to-end latency under 180 ms.

examples.title: Cascading deadline propagation in a 4-hop call tree
examples.scenario: An API gateway sets a 300 ms `grpc-timeout` on `GetCheckoutSummary`, which calls Pricing -> Promotions -> ML Fraud Scoring.
examples.outcome: gRPC automatically propagates the remaining deadline in `grpc-timeout` across each hop. When Promotions takes 280 ms, Fraud Scoring receives a 20 ms deadline and aborts early with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` (code 4) instead of burning GPU cycles for an already-abandoned request.

tradeOffs.pro: Binary Protobuf + HPACK cuts payload size by 40–70% and serialization CPU by 3–5x compared to JSON.
tradeOffs.con: Payloads are opaque on the wire; inspecting traffic requires `.proto` descriptors (`grpcurl`, Wireshark Protobuf dissector) instead of plain text logs.

tradeOffs.pro: One persistent TCP/TLS connection supports `max_concurrent_streams` (typically 100) concurrent RPCs with zero TLS handshake tax per call.
tradeOffs.con: New Kubernetes pods receive zero traffic from existing clients unless you deploy an L7 proxy (Envoy), client-side round-robin with DNS/xDS, or `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` rotation.

tradeOffs.pro: HTTP/2 `WINDOW_UPDATE` frames pause fast senders automatically when a receiver's buffer fills.
tradeOffs.con: A single stalled TCP connection (packet loss) causes TCP head-of-line blocking across all multiplexed streams on that connection.

failureModes.name: L4 load balancer hot-spotting
failureModes.description: Clients open persistent HTTP/2 connections through a Kubernetes `ClusterIP` (iptables/IPVS L4). When deployment scales from 2 to 10 pods, existing clients stay pinned to the original 2 pods.
failureModes.mitigation: Use L7 gRPC load balancing (Envoy, Istio, or gRPC client-side `round_robin` via headless DNS) and set `grpc.max_connection_age_ms` (e.g., 300,000 ms) so clients periodically rebalance.

failureModes.name: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED on large messages
failureModes.description: A service returns a 6 MB batch response, exceeding gRPC's default 4 MiB `max_receive_message_length` limit and failing with status code 8 (`RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`).
failureModes.mitigation: Convert large list responses into server-streaming RPCs (emitting 64–256 KiB chunks) rather than raising `max_receive_message_length` indefinitely.

failureModes.name: Silent keepalive disconnects (ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM)
failureModes.description: Aggressive client `keepalive_time_ms` pings (e.g., every 5 s on idle connections) trigger the server's `GOAWAY` frame with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM` (`too_many_pings`).
failureModes.mitigation: Match client `keepalive_time_ms` (>= 60 s) and `keepalive_permit_without_calls` with the server's `http2_min_recv_ping_interval_without_data_ms` policy.

failureModes.name: Breaking wire compatibility by reusing Protobuf tags
failureModes.description: A developer deletes `string legacy_id = 3;` and later adds `int64 user_id = 3;`, causing old clients to decode ASCII bytes as corrupted integers.
failureModes.mitigation: Always mark deleted tags/names with `reserved 3; reserved "legacy_id";` and gate PRs with `buf breaking --against '.git#branch=main'`.

commonMistakes: Omitting deadlines on client calls—by default gRPC has no timeout, allowing hung streams to leak goroutines/threads indefinitely.
Retrying non-idempotent mutations blindly via gRPC service config (`retryPolicy`) without idempotency keys.
Sending multi-megabyte blobs inside a single unary message instead of chunking over a client/server stream.
Using `required` semantics in `proto3` mentally—every field in `proto3` is optional on the wire and defaults to zero/empty if unset.
Assuming `http.Server` / `nginx` defaults work out of the box without enabling HTTP/2 cleartext (`h2c`) or `grpc_pass`.

sections.content:
## The idea

gRPC is an RPC framework built directly on top of **HTTP/2** and **Protocol Buffers**. Where HTTP/1.1 opens multiple TCP connections and repeats verbose text headers (`Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `User-Agent`) on every call, gRPC establishes one long-lived TCP/TLS connection and splits it into independent bidirectional **HTTP/2 streams**.

Each RPC maps to a single HTTP/2 stream ID (odd integers 1, 3, 5... initiated by the client). Request metadata travels in a `HEADERS` frame compressed with **HPACK** (reducing repeated headers to 1–2 byte table indices), serialized Protobuf messages travel in **5-byte length-prefixed `DATA` frames**, and the final RPC outcome (`grpc-status` and `grpc-message`) is delivered in a trailing `HEADERS` frame with the `END_STREAM` flag set.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a server-streaming RPC `rpc WatchMetrics(WatchRequest) returns (stream MetricPoint)` between a Go client and a Rust `tonic` server:

1. **Stream Open (`HEADERS`)**: The client allocates Stream `1` and sends `:method = POST`, `:path = /telemetry.v1.Metrics/WatchMetrics`, `content-type = application/grpc+proto`, and `grpc-timeout = 30S`.
2. **Request Payload (`DATA` + `END_STREAM`)**: The client serializes `WatchRequest{host: "prod-db-1"}` (11 bytes) with a 5-byte prefix (`0x00 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x0B`), sends it in a `DATA` frame with `END_STREAM`, half-closing its side of Stream `1`.
3. **Server Stream Emission**: The server reads `WatchRequest`, subscribes to an internal channel, and sends `HEADERS` (`:status = 200`, `content-type = application/grpc+proto`) followed by a `DATA` frame every 500 ms for each `MetricPoint`.
4. **Backpressure (`WINDOW_UPDATE`)**: If the client pauses reading for 10 seconds, its local 64 KiB stream receive buffer fills up. The client stops sending HTTP/2 `WINDOW_UPDATE` frames, forcing the server's `tonic` sender `.send().await` to suspend cleanly instead of buffering unbounded RAM.
5. **Graceful Close (`Trailers`)**: When the watch finishes (or the client sends `RST_STREAM` to cancel), the server emits trailing `HEADERS` with `grpc-status: 0` and `END_STREAM`.

sections.content:
## The four RPC streaming patterns

gRPC models all communication using four combinations of unary and streaming endpoints:

- **Unary (`Req -> Res`)**: Request-response equivalent to REST, ideal for lookups and mutations under 1 MB with strict deadlines.
- **Server Streaming (`Req -> stream Res`)**: One request opens a push feed. Replaces polling and chunked pagination for search results, log tailing, or LLM token generation.
- **Client Streaming (`stream Req -> Res`)**: Client uploads an unbounded sequence of chunks (file uploads, IoT sensor batches) and receives a single summary receipt once it half-closes the stream.
- **Bidirectional Streaming (`stream Req -> stream Res`)**: Both sides read and write independently on the same HTTP/2 stream. Because HTTP/2 frames are full-duplex, the server can push messages before the client finishes sending, enabling real-time chat, collaborative editing, and audio/video pipelines.

## Streaming transport comparison

| Feature | gRPC (HTTP/2) | REST + SSE (HTTP/1.1 or /2) | WebSockets |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Directionality** | Unary, Server, Client, Bidirectional | Server-to-client push only | Full-duplex bidirectional |
| **Contract & typing** | Strict `.proto` IDL + codegen | OpenAPI (optional) + JSON | Unstructured frames (JSON/binary) |
| **Flow control** | Built-in HTTP/2 `WINDOW_UPDATE` per stream | TCP-level only | TCP-level only (no per-topic backpressure) |
| **Browser support** | Requires gRPC-Web proxy (Envoy) | Native `EventSource` / `fetch` | Native `WebSocket` API |
| **Deadlines & cancel** | Native `grpc-timeout` + `RST_STREAM` | Manual `AbortController` / timeouts | Application-level heartbeats |

## Failure modes

- **Unbounded channel memory in async handlers**: If a server spawns a producer task that pushes into an unbounded `mpsc` queue faster than HTTP/2 `WINDOW_UPDATE` drains the socket, the server process OOMs. Always use bounded channels (`capacity = 32–128`) so backpressure propagates from the socket back to the database/Kafka reader.
- **Half-open zombie streams**: In NATed mobile networks or idle load balancers (AWS ALB/NLB idle timeout = 60–350 s), silent TCP drops leave streams stuck without `FIN`. Configure `keepalive_time_ms` + `keepalive_timeout_ms` on both client and server.
- **Retry amplification**: Enabling automatic gRPC retries for `UNAVAILABLE` without a `retryThrottling` token bucket can 3x–5x traffic during a partial outage, turning a brief blip into a sustained collapse.
- **TCP head-of-line blocking**: Because all HTTP/2 streams share one TCP connection, 2% packet loss stalls *every* active RPC on that channel until TCP retransmits.

## Deadlines, retries & health checks

Always attach a concrete deadline to every stub call (`context.WithTimeout` in Go, `withDeadlineAfter` in Java)—never rely on server-side defaults alone. Propagate incoming deadlines automatically so downstream services abort work the moment the caller's budget expires.

Implement the standard **gRPC Health Checking Protocol** (`grpc.health.v1.Health/Check` and `Watch`) so Kubernetes probes and Envoy outlier detection know when a pod is draining (`NOT_SERVING`) before closing active streams with `GOAWAY`. For retries, configure `serviceConfig` JSON only on idempotent methods (`UNAVAILABLE` with exponential backoff and `maxAttempts: 3`) and always enable `retryThrottling` (`maxTokens: 10, tokenRatio: 0.1`).

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Enforce `buf lint` and `buf breaking` in CI and mark all removed Protobuf fields with `reserved` tag numbers and names.
- [ ] Set explicit per-RPC deadlines (`grpc-timeout`) on every client call and check `ctx.Err()` / `isCancelled()` inside long-running loops.
- [ ] Use L7 load balancing (Envoy, Linkerd, or client-side xDS/`round_robin`) rather than L4 TCP balancing.
- [ ] Bound internal streaming buffers so HTTP/2 flow control (`WINDOW_UPDATE`) propagates backpressure to upstream producers.
- [ ] Align `keepalive_time_ms` and `max_connection_age_ms` across client, proxy, and server to avoid `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM` `GOAWAY` errors.
- [ ] Implement `grpc.health.v1.Health` and drain active streams gracefully on `SIGTERM` before shutting down the listener.

interviewProblems.title: gRPC & Streaming RPC
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on gRPC & Streaming RPC. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: gRPC multiplexes strongly typed Protobuf messages over persistent HTTP/2 streams, supporting unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, and full-duplex bidirectional RPCs.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Server Pod A applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Server Pod B.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Server Pod B experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use L7 gRPC load balancing (Envoy, Istio, or gRPC client-side `round_robin` via headless DNS) and set `grpc.max_connection_age_ms` (e.g., 300,000 ms) so clients periodically rebalance.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: gRPC cuts serialization and connection overhead for internal microservices and real-time streams, but HTTP/2's single-TCP-connection multiplexing breaks naive L4 load balancing.
Avoid trap: Omitting deadlines on client calls—by default gRPC has no timeout, allowing hung streams to leak goroutines/threads indefinitely.
Avoid trap: Retrying non-idempotent mutations blindly via gRPC service config (`retryPolicy`) without idempotency keys.
When to reach for it: Internal service-to-service communication in polyglot stacks (Go, Java, Python, Rust) where strict `.proto` contracts and 3–10x smaller payloads matter.
When to reach for it: Real-time streaming pipelines—live telemetry ingestion, LLM token streaming, or financial order-book ticks—using server or bidirectional streaming.

putItTogether.title: Putting Grpc Streaming Rpc Together
putItTogether.summary: gRPC cuts serialization and connection overhead for internal microservices and real-time streams, but HTTP/2's single-TCP-connection multiplexing breaks naive L4 load balancing.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Grpc Streaming Rpc before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: A single `rpc StreamTranscribe(stream AudioChunk) returns (stream TranscriptEvent)` keeps one HTTP/2 stream open. The client sends 50 frames/sec (~400 bytes each) while the server pushes interim and final transcripts on the same stream, cutting end-to-end latency under 180 ms.
